title: Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw Environmental Services
shortTitle: Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw Environmental Services
summary: Members’ reasonable avoidance of a polluted river supported standing, and deterrent civil penalties could redress violations ongoing when the citizen suit began; later compliance required a separate mootness analysis.

sections.Parties: Friends of the Earth, CLEAN, and the Sierra Club brought the citizen enforcement action. Laidlaw operated a hazardous-waste incinerator and wastewater facility discharging into South Carolina’s North Tyger River. State environmental officials had brought a separate enforcement proceeding; the United States supported the citizen plaintiffs as amicus.
sections.Material Facts: Laidlaw repeatedly exceeded its permit’s mercury limits; the district court found 489 violations between 1987 and 1995. Nearby members described curtailed fishing, swimming, camping, and other uses because of reasonable concerns about the discharges. After the organizations gave the required 60-day notice, Laidlaw asked the state to sue, its lawyer drafted the complaint, and it paid the filing fee. A settlement for$100,000 was reached just before the notice period ended. The district court later found that prosecution insufficiently diligent to bar the citizen suit. Violations continued after the citizen complaint, though Laidlaw later substantially complied and reported closing the facility.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied Laidlaw’s standing-based summary-judgment motion and its request to dismiss based on the state prosecution. It imposed a$405,800 civil penalty after finding more than$1 million in economic benefit from noncompliance, but denied an injunction. Plaintiffs appealed the penalty amount; Laidlaw cross-appealed on standing and the state-prosecution bar. The Fourth Circuit assumed initial standing but found mootness because penalties payable to the government supposedly could not redress the plaintiffs. It vacated and ordered dismissal. The Supreme Court rejected that approach, found initial standing, and required a distinct mootness inquiry. Attorney-fee entitlement was left to the district court in the first instance.
sections.Issue: Whether evidence of diminished recreational use established personal injury despite a lack of demonstrated environmental damage; whether Treasury-paid penalties could redress ongoing injury; and whether subsequent compliance or closure eliminated the controversy.
sections.Holding: The plaintiffs established standing to pursue penalties for violations ongoing at filing. Their reasonable curtailed use supplied injury, and the penalties’ deterrent effect could redress continuing and future harms. Subsequent voluntary cessation did not automatically moot the case. The Court did not itself decide the fee application or resolve an independently presented Article II challenge.
sections.Reasoning: The majority distinguished the plaintiff’s injury from environmental damage as such. Specific members connected their reduced use to a particular river and concededly ongoing permit violations, unlike vague geographic or speculative future-use allegations. Each remedy still required standing, but penalties could reduce ongoing harm by making future noncompliance less attractive. Steel Co.’s wholly past violations were different because their cessation preceded suit. For later cessation, the defendant bore a heavy burden to show recurrence could not reasonably be expected; standing’s initial inquiry could not simply be reapplied as an automatic mootness rule. Scalia, joined by Thomas, disputed the proof of actual personal harm where environmental studies showed no demonstrated damage, rejected generalized deterrence as private redress, and criticized transferring enforcement leverage to private plaintiffs. Kennedy’s omitted concurrence, summarized by the editors, reserved Article II questions. These limits prevent treating the case as an unrestricted authorization for private enforcement or a complete resolution of facility-closure facts.
